analysis.one_liner: Imposes federal consumer protections on sports betting: deposit limits, affordability checks, ad restrictions, and a national self-exclusion list.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received no hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reverse the current free-for-all in which dozens of states run their own sports betting rules. It would make accepting a sports bet illegal nationwide unless a state applies to the Justice Department and agrees to a list of federal standards: no betting before age 21, a cap of five deposits a day, no credit-card deposits, affordability checks above $1,000 a day, bans on advertising during most daytime hours and during live games, no AI-driven targeting of individual bettors, and a national self-exclusion list a person can join to block themselves everywhere. It would also fund an annual federal survey of problem gambling and a national gambling-addiction surveillance system.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports, or who are vulnerable to losing control of their betting. The bill limits how much money can go in the door at once, bans credit-card-funded betting, stops operators from using AI to target individuals with promotions, requires clear disclosure of bonus terms, bars operators from withholding winnings or imposing withdrawal limits, and creates a national list so a person who wants to stop can be blocked at every legal operator in one step. People with gambling disorder would also gain from federally funded treatment, education, and better data on the problem.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sports bettors and people at risk of gambling addiction

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps deposits at five per 24 hours, bans credit-card deposits, and requires affordability checks before accepting more than $1,000 in a day or $10,000 in 30 days, verified against income or a standard consumer-lending check.

It bars operators from using artificial intelligence to track individual wagers, target specific people with offers, or build products like microbets, and bans advertising between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. and during live game broadcasts.

It creates a national self-exclusion list that blocks a person from betting with any operator in any participating state, and requires operators to fund treatment for gambling disorder and responsible-gaming education.

It bans betting by anyone under 21, by athletes, coaches, officials, and credentialed staff on their own events, and proposition bets on amateur and college sports, and requires operators to report suspicious transactions to regulators and sports leagues.

It directs the Department of Health and Human Services to run an annual nationwide survey of problem gambling (not conducted or funded by the gambling industry), a national gambling-addiction surveillance system, and a Surgeon General's report on the public health effects of widespread sports betting.

analysis.who_pays: Sports betting companies and their investors bear the direct cost: advertising restrictions that reach most of the day, bans on bonus-style promotions, deposit and affordability limits, mandatory treatment funding, reserve requirements, and background-check and recordkeeping obligations. States that run betting programs would have to apply to the Justice Department and rework their rules to meet the federal standards, and any state that does not or cannot apply would see betting become illegal there, costing those states tax revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sports betting companies and some state programs

drawbacks.text: The bill does not merely add protections — it makes accepting a sports bet illegal everywhere unless a state applies for and wins Justice Department approval under the new standards, and betting only takes effect 18 months after enactment, so existing state programs could shut down if they fail to qualify.

A state's program is only valid for a fixed three-year term, subject to renewal and to emergency revocation by the Attorney General, which puts an executive-branch official in a recurring gatekeeping role over a legal activity states currently regulate themselves.

Affordability checks would require bettors exceeding the deposit thresholds to have income verified or to pass a consumer-lending-style check, which many customers would see as an intrusion into their privacy for a legal activity.

Advertising would be barred during nearly all waking hours and during live games, and operators could not use words like "bonus" or explain how bets work in ads, restrictions that reach protected commercial speech and would sharply cut the industry's main customer-acquisition channel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections aim at real, documented harms: online sports betting is engineered for rapid repeat deposits, and the industry's growth model relies on heavy bettors, many of whom develop gambling disorder. Deposit limits, a national self-exclusion list, and an end to AI-targeted promotions would genuinely help that group, and federal surveillance of gambling addiction is currently missing. The cost side is real too: the bill would upend legal betting in the roughly three dozen states that already run programs by forcing them through a federal approval process with a three-year clock and Attorney General discretion, and the blanket ban on nearly all sports-betting advertising is a blunt tool that goes well past the misleading-ad problem. The core protections are well targeted; the federal prohibition-and-approval architecture is the weakest part of the design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in September 2024 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on September 16, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sports betting operators came out ahead: none of the deposit limits, affordability checks, advertising bans, or AI-targeting restrictions in the bill were ever enacted, so betting companies keep their existing state-by-state rules, their daytime ad schedules, their bonus promotions, and their ability to target individual bettors with offers. People who struggle with betting also got nothing, as no federal problem-gambling survey or treatment funding followed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sports betting companies and their investors

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the bill lists no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it dead at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Commercial sports betting industry
against.role: Operators of the major online sportsbooks
against.what_they_did: The major sportsbooks depend on heavy advertising, bonus promotions, and rapid repeat deposits, and their industry has opposed federal restrictions of this kind; no operator or trade group supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its only supporter was a single Democratic senator with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill's profitability model — all-day advertising, bonus promotions, AI-targeted offers, credit-card and rapid repeat deposits, and revenue concentrated among heavy bettors — is exactly what the bill restricts or bans. Operators would also have to fund gambling-disorder treatment and maintain reserves covering customer funds. The industry's gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued exposure to those practices.

The bill gives sports organizations the right to request that regulators restrict or bar wagers on their events to protect contest integrity, requires operators to share suspicious-transaction reports with leagues, and bans proposition bets on amateur and college sports. League integrity staff get more tools to detect suspicious betting.

The bill requires operators to settle wagers only using data from sources approved by the state regulator, initially limited to league-licensed data, creating a protected, regulated market for official data feeds. Bettors benefit from accurate settlement; the licensed-data structure channels revenue to approved providers.

The bill preserves state and tribal authority, lets tribes join interstate betting compacts approved by the Attorney General, and deems online wagers to occur where the server sits — a rule that benefits tribes hosting servers on Indian lands under a tribal-state compact. Tribes would face the same federal standards as states.

The bill bans the use of credit cards to fund betting deposits, cutting off a source of interest-earning revolving debt tied to gambling losses. Bettors are protected from borrowing to bet; issuers lose that volume.
